title: Umbrella, specialty liability, bonds, surplus lines and flood
summary: Umbrella vs excess, professional and other specialty liability, surety bonds, Michigan surplus lines, NFIP flood, and self-insured retentions.
objectives: Tell umbrella from excess and match specialty liability coverages to claims
Name the three parties to a surety bond and the main bond types
Know Michigan's surplus lines rules and the NFIP limits, wait and deductibles
Explain how a self-insured retention differs from a deductible

scenes.title: Other coverages and options
scenes.subtitle: Umbrella and excess, specialty liability, surety bonds, surplus lines, flood and self-insurance

beats.text: Other coverages are 4% of your exam, about 6 questions.
beats.say: Other coverages are four percent of your exam, about six questions.

scenes.title: Umbrella vs excess liability
scenes.src: IRMI glossary 'umbrella liability policy', 'follow form', 'excess liability policy'

columns.name: Umbrella
points: Adds limits when underlying limits are used up
Drops down when an underlying aggregate is exhausted
Covers some claims the underlying doesn't, after a self-insured retention

columns.name: Excess (follow form)
points: Generally follows the underlying policy's terms

scenes.tell: Can it pay a claim the primary policy doesn't cover? Umbrella. Does it only add limits? Excess.

beats.text: An umbrella adds limits when underlying limits run out, drops down when an underlying aggregate is exhausted, and covers some claims the underlying doesn't, after a self-insured retention.
beats.say: An umbrella adds limits when underlying limits run out, drops down when an underlying aggregate is exhausted, and covers some claims the underlying doesn't, after a self-insured retention.

beats.text: An excess, or follow form, policy generally follows the underlying terms and adds limits. It doesn't broaden coverage.
beats.say: An excess, or follow form, policy generally follows the underlying terms and adds limits. It doesn't broaden coverage.

scenes.title: Specialty liability: match the claim
scenes.src: IRMI glossary (E&O; Side A, corporate reimbursement, entity coverage; fiduciary liability; EPLI); ISO CG 00 33 04 13; MCL 436.1803(1)
items: A client's financial loss from a mistake
A: D&Os. B: company reimbursed. C: entity
Errors running ERISA employee benefit plans
Injury from selling or serving alcohol

beats.text: Errors and omissions generally covers financial loss from a professional mistake, not bodily injury or property damage.
beats.say: Errors and omissions generally covers financial loss from a professional mistake, not bodily injury or property damage.

beats.text: D&O: Side A pays directors and officers directly, Side B reimburses the company for indemnifying them, and Side C covers the company itself.
beats.say: D and O: Side A pays directors and officers directly, Side B reimburses the company for indemnifying them, and Side C covers the company itself.

beats.text: Fiduciary liability covers errors in running ERISA employee benefit plans.
beats.say: Fiduciary liability covers errors in running E R I S A employee benefit plans.

beats.text: EPLI covers employment claims like discrimination, harassment and wrongful termination.
beats.say: E P L I covers employment claims like discrimination, harassment and wrongful termination.

beats.text: Liquor liability covers injury from selling or serving alcohol. Michigan retail liquor licensees must file proof of financial responsibility of at least $50,000.
beats.say: Liquor liability covers injury from selling or serving alcohol. Michigan retail liquor licensees must file proof of financial responsibility of at least fifty thousand dollars.

scenes.q: Jen, a producer, forgets to add a client's newly bought warehouse to his property policy. It burns, and he sues her for the uninsured loss. Which coverage is designed for this claim?
scenes.why: The claim is a client's financial loss caused by a mistake in Jen's professional duties, which is what errors and omissions insurance is designed to cover.

beats.text: Jen, a producer, forgets to add a client's new warehouse to his property policy. It burns, and he sues her. Which coverage is designed for this? Pick an answer.
beats.say: Jen, a producer, forgets to add a client's new warehouse to his property policy. It burns, and he sues her. Which coverage is designed for this? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: Errors and omissions. The client's financial loss came from a mistake in Jen's professional duties.
reveal.say: Errors and omissions. The client's financial loss came from a mistake in Jen's professional duties.

scenes.title: Professional liability vs the CGL
scenes.src: IRMI glossary 'professional liability', 'claims-made policy', 'defense within limits', 'consent to settlement clause'; ISO CG 00 01 04 13

columns.name: Professional liability
points: Defense costs reduce the limit (shrinking limits)
Insurer must seek your consent to settle (hammer clause)

columns.name: CGL
points: Defense paid in addition to the limits
Insurer may settle at its discretion

scenes.tell: Professional liability: claims-made, shrinking limits, and your consent to settle.

beats.text: Most professional liability policies are claims-made: a claim made during the policy period triggers them, whenever the error happened.
beats.say: Most professional liability policies are claims-made: a claim made during the policy period triggers them, whenever the error happened.

beats.text: Defense costs usually reduce the limit, called shrinking limits. And under a consent to settlement, or hammer, clause, the insurer must seek your approval before settling.
beats.say: Defense costs usually reduce the limit, called shrinking limits. And under a consent to settlement, or hammer, clause, the insurer must seek your approval before settling.

beats.text: In a CGL, defense is paid on top of the limits, and the insurer may settle at its discretion.
beats.say: In a C G L, defense is paid on top of the limits, and the insurer may settle at its discretion.

scenes.title: Surety bonds: three parties
scenes.src: FAR 48 CFR 28.001 'Bond'; surety.org; SFAA and AGC surety claims guide; IRMI glossary 'surety bond', 'obligee'

columns.name: Principal
points: Promises to perform, like a contractor
Must reimburse the surety for losses

columns.name: Obligee
points: Protected party, like the project owner

scenes.tell: The principal promises, the obligee is protected, the surety guarantees.

beats.text: A surety bond has three parties. The principal, like a contractor, promises to perform.
beats.say: A surety bond has three parties. The principal, like a contractor, promises to perform.

beats.text: The obligee, like the project owner, is protected. It usually requires the bond.
beats.say: The obligee, like the project owner, is protected. It usually requires the bond.

beats.text: The surety guarantees the promise. Unlike insurance, the principal must reimburse the surety for any loss it pays.
beats.say: The surety guarantees the promise. Unlike insurance, the principal must reimburse the surety for any loss it pays.

scenes.title: Bond types and what they guarantee
scenes.src: FAR 48 CFR 28.001; IRMI 'license and permit bond', 'fiduciary bond'; FC&S 'Judicial Bonds' (2000), 'License and Permit Bonds' (2010)
items: Bidder will sign and furnish the bonds
Labor and material suppliers get paid
Licensee will comply with the law
Damages or costs if the court action fails

beats.text: Contract bonds: a bid bond guarantees the bidder will sign the contract and furnish the required bonds; a performance bond, that the contract is performed; a payment bond, that labor and material suppliers get paid.
beats.say: Contract bonds: a bid bond guarantees the bidder will sign the contract and furnish the required bonds; a performance bond, that the contract is performed; a payment bond, that labor and material suppliers get paid.

beats.text: A license and permit bond guarantees a licensee will comply with the laws for its activity.
beats.say: A license and permit bond guarantees a licensee will comply with the laws for its activity.

beats.text: Judicial bonds come in two classes: fiduciary bonds, for people the court trusts with others' property, and court bonds, like an attachment or injunction bond, which pay if the bonded party's court action fails.
beats.say: Judicial bonds come in two classes: fiduciary bonds, for people the court trusts with others' property, and court bonds, like an attachment or injunction bond, which pay if the bonded party's court action fails.

scenes.q: A township won't issue a business license until the applicant posts a bond guaranteeing it will follow township ordinances. Who is the obligee?
choices: The business applying for the license
The producer who arranged the bond
scenes.why: On a license and permit bond, the government body that requires the bond and is protected by it is the obligee. The applicant is the principal; the surety guarantees.

beats.text: A township won't issue a business license until the applicant posts a bond promising to follow its ordinances. Who's the obligee? Pick an answer.
beats.say: A township won't issue a business license until the applicant posts a bond promising to follow its ordinances. Who's the obligee? Pick an answer.

reveal.text: The township: it requires the bond and is protected by it. The applicant is the principal.
reveal.say: The township: it requires the bond and is protected by it. The applicant is the principal.

scenes.title: Surplus lines in Michigan
scenes.src: MCL 500.1903(1); 500.1905(1),(3)(d); 500.1910(1)-(3); 500.1922 (federal NRRA home-state rules not reviewed)

items.label: Unauthorized but eligible insurer
items.detail: Not licensed in Michigan; placed only by a surplus lines licensee

items.label: Only if admitted insurers won't write it
items.detail: Presumed available if 3 or more authorized insurers readily write it

items.label: Red-ink notice, 10-point type
items.detail: Insurer not licensed by Michigan; claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent

items.label: 2% tax plus 0.5% fee
items.detail: Set by Michigan statute; paid by the licensee

beats.text: Surplus lines insurers aren't licensed in Michigan but are eligible to write here, through a surplus lines licensee.
beats.say: Surplus lines insurers aren't licensed in Michigan but are eligible to write here, through a surplus lines licensee.

beats.text: It's only for coverage authorized insurers won't provide; if 3 or more readily write it, it's presumed available.
beats.say: It's only for coverage authorized insurers won't provide; if three or more readily write it, it's presumed available.

beats.text: Each policy carries a red-ink notice in at least 10-point type: the insurer isn't licensed by Michigan, and claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent.
beats.say: Each policy carries a red-ink notice in at least ten-point type: the insurer isn't licensed by Michigan, and claims may not be guaranteed if it's insolvent.

beats.text: Under Michigan's statute, the licensee pays a 2% tax plus a 0.5% regulatory fee.
beats.say: Under Michigan's statute, the licensee pays a two percent tax plus a zero point five percent regulatory fee.

scenes.title: Flood: NFIP limits and the wait
scenes.src: 44 CFR 61.6; 44 CFR Pt. 61 App. A(1) III.D; FEMA brochures (07-2024; 01-2024); floodsmart.gov; amounts can change
scenes.hook: Homes: 250 and 100. Businesses: 500 and 500. Code compliance: 30 grand. The wait: 30 days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.
items: Increased Cost of Compliance: up to $30,000, within the building maximum
Wait: typically 30 days; none when bought in connection with a loan

beats.text: Now the National Flood Insurance Program. The hook: homes, 250 and 100. Businesses, 500 and 500. Code compliance, 30 grand. The wait, 30 days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.
beats.say: Now the National Flood Insurance Program. The hook: homes, two hundred fifty and one hundred. Businesses, five hundred and five hundred. Code compliance, thirty grand. The wait, thirty days, but none when you buy it as part of a loan closing.

beats.text: Homes, meaning single-family and 2 to 4 family, get $250,000 building and $100,000 contents. Non-residential gets $500,000 each.
beats.say: Homes, meaning single-family and two to four family, get two hundred fifty thousand dollars building and one hundred thousand dollars contents. Non-residential gets five hundred thousand dollars each.

beats.text: Increased Cost of Compliance adds up to $30,000 to elevate, demolish, relocate or floodproof, but building plus that payment can't exceed the building maximum.
beats.say: Increased Cost of Compliance adds up to thirty thousand dollars to elevate, demolish, relocate or floodproof, but building plus that payment can't exceed the building maximum.

beats.text: The loan exception covers making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan.
beats.say: The loan exception covers making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan.

scenes.title: NFIP: who sells it, other exceptions, deductibles
scenes.src: 44 CFR 61.11; FEMA brochure (07-2024); agents.floodsmart.gov 'Flood Insurance 101'; FEMA RR2.0 Simple Guide (deductibles; can change)

items.label: NFIP Direct or Write Your Own (WYO)
items.detail: WYO: private insurers write and service it in their own names; the government pays all losses

items.label: Other exceptions to the 30-day wait
items.detail: Added coverage on a renewal bill. Newly mapped into an SFHA: 1-day wait if bought within 13 months

items.label: Flooding on burned federal land
items.detail: 1-day wait if bought within 60 days of fire containment

items.label: Minimum deductibles (Risk Rating 2.0)
items.detail: Residential, no pre-FIRM discount: building $1,000 if $100,000 or less, $1,250 if more; contents $1,000

beats.text: Write Your Own companies are private insurers that write and service policies in their own names; the federal government pays all losses. Coverage matches NFIP Direct.
beats.say: Write Your Own companies are private insurers that write and service policies in their own names; the federal government pays all losses. Coverage matches N F I P Direct.

beats.text: Other exceptions: added coverage on a renewal bill, and a 1-day wait for a building newly mapped into a special flood hazard area.
beats.say: Other exceptions: added coverage on a renewal bill, and a one-day wait for a building newly mapped into a special flood hazard area.

beats.text: For flooding on burned federal land, the wait is 1 day if you buy within 60 days of fire containment.
beats.say: For flooding on burned federal land, the wait is one day if you buy within sixty days of fire containment.

beats.text: FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0 minimum deductibles, which can change: for a residential building with no pre-FIRM discount, $1,000 if coverage is $100,000 or less, $1,250 if more. Contents: a separate $1,000.
beats.say: FEMA's Risk Rating two point zero minimum deductibles, which can change: for a residential building with no pre-firm discount, one thousand dollars if coverage is one hundred thousand dollars or less, one thousand two hundred fifty dollars if more. Contents: a separate one thousand dollars.

items.label: SIR: insured pays first
items.expr: Defense and damages up to the SIR

beats.text: Last, self-insurance: a formal decision to retain risk and pay losses from a set-aside fund. Here's a self-insured retention versus a deductible.
beats.say: Last, self-insurance: a formal decision to retain risk and pay losses from a set-aside fund. Here's a self-insured retention versus a deductible.

beats.text: With an SIR of $25,000, the insured pays the first $25,000 itself, and the insurer pays the other $75,000.
beats.say: With an S I R of twenty-five thousand dollars, the insured pays the first twenty-five thousand dollars itself, and the insurer pays the other seventy-five thousand dollars.

beats.text: With a deductible of $25,000, the insurer pays all $100,000, then bills the insured $25,000.
beats.say: With a deductible of twenty-five thousand dollars, the insurer pays all one hundred thousand dollars, then bills the insured twenty-five thousand dollars.

E&O and most professional liability: financial loss, claims-made
Bonds: principal promises, obligee protected, surety guarantees
